R_H1.passageTitle: Visiting Japanese Shrines and Temples Respectfully

passages.label: A
passages.text: The appearance of an entrance can offer the first clue to what people expect inside, and many Japanese shrines have a torii gate. A temple may have a Sanmon gate and guardian statues. Each serves a separate faith, Shinto belief or the Buddhist tradition, and this is one aspect of Japanese culture a traveller can see in a brief visit, as long as they treat both places as spaces for serious religious use.

passages.label: B
passages.text: At a shrine, visitors commonly bow once before passing through the gate and continue just to one side rather than taking the central route. These actions express respect as part of entering the sacred space. Observing the suggested path matters even if walking through the centre would seem more direct to someone unfamiliar with the custom.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Before proceeding inside a shrine, visitors may find a temizuya, or water pavilion. Purification, or cleansing, follows a clear order. First, use the right hand to hold the ladle and pour water over the left hand, so the left hand is washed first. Next, change hands and wash the right hand. Finally, pour water into the left hand, rinse the mouth, and spit beside the fountain, and the ladle must never touch the mouth directly. Each hand therefore has a separate role at different points in the process.

passages.label: D
passages.text: At a shrine altar, or prayer place, the ceremony has a detailed sequence. Toss a coin into the offering box and ring the bell to greet the shrine’s god. Bow twice, clap twice, and then say a prayer. Finish by bowing once more before leaving so the next worshipper can approach. The number and order of these actions matter because they distinguish shrine practice from temple prayer. Following the steps carefully is more useful than copying only the most visible movement, and the signs at an entrance can provide an obvious place to start.

passages.label: E
passages.text: At a Buddhist altar, a visitor makes an offering and brings the hands together in silent prayer. A family attending a ceremony may know certain actions from experience, while a visitor can look for a sign or watch a common local practice. Where a temple has a water pavilion, the cleansing step may resemble part of a shrine visit. The main acts of prayer still differ. A more formal setting calls for extra care when people greet one another or move around a shrine or temple.

passages.label: F
passages.text: Thoughtful conduct can help people interact without disturbing someone making a personal visit. A traditional action may be appropriate on one occasion, while acceptable behaviour in another place can be different. Signs give helpful instructions about removing shoes on entering certain rooms and speaking quietly near places used for worship. These requirements can arise from the layout of the sanctuary, the circulation of visitors or a need to limit interruptions during worship. A social outing still carries an obligation to respect ceremonial spaces and other visitors’ privacy. A thoughtful visitor observes local expectations before entering unfamiliar parts of the precinct.

R_H2.passageTitle: Preparing for Business Meetings in Brazil

passages.label: A
passages.text: The 2019 Investment Guide to Brasil from Brazil’s Ministry of Economy says business etiquette is not particularly different from practices in North America or Europe, although several aspects deserve attention. It describes Brazilian hosts as communicative and warm. Outside the workplace, the culture is often informal, and kindness and good humour are usually viewed as good manners. In business, interpersonal relationships can matter, so being communicative can be productive. And these are general patterns rather than rules for every person or organisation.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Portuguese is Brazil’s official language. And the guide stresses that it differs considerably from Spanish, and visitors should not expect English or Spanish to be understood, especially outside major cities. Brazilian hosts often appreciate an effort to say a few words in Portuguese, and a visitor who does not speak Portuguese should tell the host. Because language and culture vary between regions, the guide recommends travelling with a local guide or researching the specific region before the visit.

passages.label: C
passages.text: At business introductions, handshakes with women and men are common. Hugs may occur after people have developed some familiarity, but they are unlikely during introductions. International business clothing is the normal dress code, and business cards are regularly exchanged, and a visitor can greet a new contact warmly while still allowing their connection to develop. A professional appearance and a handshake fit the source guidance, whereas assuming that a hug is required does not.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Brazilians often use first names from the beginning of contact, but this does not prove familiarity. Titles such as Senhor, Senhora and Doutor can appear before a first name. An email is acceptable when first contacting a medium-sized or large company. The guide also recommends making at least one phone call before the meeting. Business contacts should normally choose the meeting place. If the choice belongs to the visitor, restaurants and cafés are possible because meetings often occur in less formal environments.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A serious appointment is also a matter of planning. The guide describes traffic in São Paulo and Rio as a reason to allow time for travel. Leave room between separate meetings, because a brief conversation can grow into a longer one. It may be obvious to hosts that their workday can change, but a visitor should confirm the current plan. Asking about a certain time or place in advance can help preserve the relationship without treating one guide as a rule for every organisation or tradition.

passages.label: F
passages.text: A commercial meeting is also a situation where people interact as individuals. A written agreement can clarify an obligation, while social contact may help people develop trust. In a multicultural workplace, acceptable behaviour can differ between teams. It is helpful to notice when a colleague prefers to keep a matter personal. A thoughtful question about local practice is more useful than assuming that a description applies on every occasion.

passages.label: A
passages.text: In 2022, UNESCO listed China's traditional tea processing and related social practices as intangible cultural heritage. And the practice includes growing, picking, processing and serving tea. A formal ceremony uses tea in one way, whereas the a usual way to do this of making tea to greet a guest serves a different purpose. As people exchange ideas about working with the leaves or make time to talk over a cup, these aspects of culture help create relationships.

passages.label: B
passages.text: UNESCO describes six categories: green, yellow, dark, white, oolong and black tea. With reprocessed varieties such as flower-scented teas included, UNESCO reports more than 2,000 products. They differ in colour, smell, taste and shape. The differences depend on growing conditions as well as the choices tea makers make. A worker may watch the colour of a leaf change before deciding that it is ready for the next step. To understand how this variety comes about, learners need to observe what happens between picking the leaves and serving the tea.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Tea is served steeped or boiled in homes, workplaces, tea houses, restaurants and temples. UNESCO describes it as part of socialisation and of ceremonies such as weddings and sacrifices. Tea-related activities can greet guests and build relationships within families and among neighbours. The practice is common to multiple ethnic groups and can provide communities with a sense of shared identity and continuity. These are broad patterns rather than one rule for every person. A formal event and an ordinary conversation can both involve tea, while the exact preparation and meaning can vary by setting.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The knowledge and skills are passed on through families and apprenticeships. UNESCO identifies tea producers, farmers, artists and pastry makers as bearers of the practice. Their different roles show that passing on skills involves a network rather than just one occupation. Teaching connects one generation with the next, but learners also need chances to observe, repeat and apply what they learn. To preserve a living skill, communities must keep it usable. Written records can help, although learning between people remains central to continuity.

passages.label: E
passages.text: An award can make the practice more obvious to visitors, but protection involves serious work after that. A brief display can introduce people to certain tools and techniques. A separate question is whether learners can practise with someone who knows the work. If a generation only sees a finished product for sale, it may have little chance to learn how to make it. The committee also drew attention to the effects of commercial use. Helping people preserve the practice takes time and people who are ready to teach. A person who can already prepare tea in one way may be in a good position to learn another. A traditional practice can strengthen social ties. People interact on an ordinary occasion or at a commercial event. A personal lesson gives someone a chance to learn by using their hands. Teachers can modernise a way to teach and let older skills live on.
